messages.content: Explain in exactly three sentences why floating-point addition is not associative.
Explain in exactly three sentences why floating-point addition is not associative.

samples.text: In floating‑point arithmetic each number is stored with a limited number of bits, so after an addition the exact real result must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Because this rounding occurs after every intermediate operation, the accumulated rounding error depends on how the operands are grouped. Therefore \((a+b)+c\) and \(a+(b+c)\) can be rounded to different values, demonstrating that floating‑point addition is not associative.

In floating‑point arithmetic each operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value because numbers are stored with a finite number of bits. This rounding can change the magnitude of an intermediate result, so adding a and b first and then adding c may yield a different rounded value than adding b and c first and then adding a. Consequently, \((a+b)+c\neq a+(b+c)\) in general, demonstrating that floating‑point addition is not associative.

Consequently, \((a+b)+c\) and \(a+(b+c)\) may yield different floating‑point values, demonstrating that addition is not associative.
